chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
title: Selling newspapers as a boy
summary: At ten or eleven he sold the Item for a penny on Washington Avenue, later the Louisiana Weekly, earning pennies for rent of a dollar a month.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I remember mostly the white bands. I didn't see a Zulu parade until I was in my teens. See, because my mother kept close watch on me most of the time. I was in my teens. By her and my father being separated because I can remember when I was about 10, 11 years of age, my mother took sick and I called myself helping her. And there was some white guy in the neighborhood and I went up on Washington Avenue to sell the evening edition when I got out of school of the old, what's that, the old item newspaper. That's when the paper was one penny, one cent. A lot of people don't remember that. You don't either. One cent. The paper was one penny.
Was this a part-time job you had?

That was a part-time job I had with a kid during the summer. And as I would make the little money, I would bring it home to my mother. And I can remember when we were living at 515 Third Street, you wouldn't believe this. The rent was $1 a month, 25 cents a week. Wasn't that something?
What kind of money would you make with the newspaper?
I was making like maybe 12 cents a day, 15 cents a day or something. When I made 25 cents on the weekend, that was big money.
And you had, did you stand in a corner?
You know, with the automobile. It was passing.
Which corner was that? Do you remember?

That was up on Annunciation and Washington Avenue. One of those corners. Then I think one time I think I moved over to Chapitula Street, but some guy ran me from over there. Boy, you can't stand out here.
Did you get to choose where you stood? I mean,

Well, I didn't have an especially arrangement to sell where you could. I just was working all over the area. Didn't have no, well, you know, for black folks at that particular time, you go back 1930s and 40s, you didn't have no designated area. You just sold what you could where you could. Sometimes I knock on doors with people to sell the paper, you know. Then as I started getting a little early, older, I went downtown and started selling the Louisiana Weekly. Today, I guess you can say I'm...
Now you're writing for the Weekly.
Something like a wheel with the Louisiana Over 25, quarter of a century. Yeah.
